misconception_description: Student believes that values must be explicitly converted to their current type to ensure type safety.

solutions.generated_code:
program HitungInversi
kamus
  a, b, c, jumlah : integer
algoritma
  input(a, b, c)
  a <- integer(a)
  b <- integer(b)
  c <- integer(c)
  jumlah <- integer(0)
  if integer(a) > integer(b) then
    jumlah <- integer(jumlah) + 1
  endif
  if integer(a) > integer(c) then
    jumlah <- integer(jumlah) + 1
  endif
  if integer(b) > integer(c) then
    jumlah <- integer(jumlah) + 1
  endif
  output(integer(jumlah))
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student has added explicit int() conversions throughout the code to ensure "type safety". They convert: inv_count to int when initializing with 0, i and j to int when using them as indices (even though range() already returns integers), the literal 1 to int when incrementing and calculating the range, inv_count to int before adding to it, and the return value to int. The student genuinely believes these conversions are necessary and good practice for ensuring variables maintain their correct type. While inefficient and unnecessary, the code still functions correctly since converting an integer to an integer is a no-op that doesn't change the value or cause errors.
